summary: Describes how to identify the various protocol encapsulations that the Remote Network Monitoring MIB version 2 manages. It was replaced by RFC 2895.

eli5.summary: It is a naming system so a network monitor can say what kind of traffic it saw.

questions: how to name protocols in rmon
subtitle: A naming system for how network protocols stack together in RMON monitoring.

tldr.problem: RMON (Remote Network Monitoring) needs a way to uniquely identify and name the different ways protocols stack on top of each other (for example, Ethernet, then IP, then TCP, then HTTP), so a monitoring agent can report what traffic it is seeing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2074 defines protocol-identifier encoding: each protocol layer is encoded as a 4-octet value, and protocol encapsulations are identified by concatenating these layer-identifiers into a string. It also provides a macro format for naming new protocol combinations.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was replaced by RFC 2895 with updates and clarifications.

today: RFC 2074 was superseded by RFC 2895, which provides updated protocol identifier definitions.

sections.title: Introduction and RMON Context
sections.content:
RMON (Remote Network Monitoring) is a management framework that allows network devices to collect, monitor, and report on network traffic. RMON-2 extends RMON to monitor protocols at multiple layers of the network stack, not just the data link layer.

To report on traffic, RMON needs a standard way to name and identify protocol encapsulations. For example, "traffic using HTTP over TCP over IP over Ethernet" is a different encapsulation than "traffic using SNMP over UDP over IP over PPP." RFC 2074 defines the encoding scheme and naming convention for these protocol stacks.
sections.eli5: When a network monitor watches traffic flowing by, it sees all kinds of stacks of protocols nested inside each other. It needs names for all these different combinations so it can say "I saw this kind of traffic."

sections.title: Hierarchical Protocol Encoding
sections.content:
In RFC 2074, a protocol encapsulation is identified using a hierarchical structure. The lowest layer is always a base protocol (for example, Ethernet, LLC, or SNAP). Above that sit child protocols at higher layers (for example, IP, IPX, or AppleTalk at layer 3; TCP or UDP at layer 4; HTTP, SNMP, or Telnet at layer 5 and above).

Each protocol layer is encoded as a 4-octet (32-bit) value in network byte order, except for SNAP encapsulations which use 8 octets. A complete protocol-identifier is an octet string containing one or more of these layer-identifiers, starting from the base protocol and working upward through the stack.
sections.eli5: You describe a stack of protocols by starting at the bottom and working up. Ethernet, then IP, then TCP, then HTTP is one stack. Change any layer, and it is a different stack with a different name.

sections.title: Encoding Scheme and Examples
sections.content:
Each 4-octet layer-identifier is encoded as a sequence of four sub-identifiers (one per octet). For example, Ethernet (base value 1) is encoded as 1.0.0.0. IP (value 2048, hex 0800) over Ethernet would be encoded as 1.0.0.0 followed by 8.0.0.0, creating a combined identifier for the Ethernet-IP stack.

The RFC provides concrete examples: HTTP over IP over Ethernet encodes as 16.0.0.0.1.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.6.0.0.0.80 (the .80 at the end is the TCP port for HTTP). SNMP over UDP/IP over SNAP (a variant of Ethernet) encodes as 16.0.0.0.3.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.17.0.0.0.161, where .161 is the UDP port for SNMP.
sections.eli5: Each layer gets a 4-number code like 8.0.0.0 for IP or 6.0.0.0 for TCP. Stack them together to name the whole sandwich: Ethernet, then IP, then TCP, then HTTP becomes one long list of numbers.

sections.title: Protocol Identifiers and Parameters
sections.content:
RFC 2074 also defines a macro format for naming protocol-identifier combinations and describing their properties. Each protocol-identifier macro has a name (such as ether2.ip.tcp.http), a list of configuration parameters (bits that describe special functions or capabilities of the protocol), and attributes describing how the protocol encodes and what child protocols it can carry.

The macro format includes sections for CHILDREN (what protocols can be nested inside this one), ADDRESS-FORMAT (how source and destination addresses are identified), DECODING (hints on how to parse the protocol), and REFERENCE (citations to authoritative documents like RFCs). This allows the protocol-identifier document to be extended with new protocols and variants without updating the RMON MIB code itself.
sections.eli5: For each protocol name, you write down: what can go inside it, how to find the source and destination, how to decode it, and where the official definition is. That way, monitors everywhere can learn new protocols without reprogramming.

sections.title: Base Protocols and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
RFC 2074 defines a set of base-layer protocols: Ethernet (with a flag for raw or 802.3 variants), LLC (Logical Link Control), SNAP with different Organizational Unit Identifiers (OUIs), and IANA-assigned protocols. The base layer identifies the lowest protocol in the stack, the one that carries all higher layers.

IANA-assigned protocols are used for encapsulations that cannot be practically identified by examining network traffic. These are encoded differently and have a separate macro format (protocol-variant-identifier) to document them. This allows the document to remain open to new protocols without being updated every time a new layer 3 or layer 4 protocol is assigned.
sections.eli5: The bottom layer is always something standard like Ethernet or SNAP. If an encapsulation is weird or rare, it gets a special entry at IANA (the registry) instead of a regular name.

sections.title: Relationship to RMON-2 MIB
sections.content:
This document is intentionally separated from the RMON-2 MIB specification to allow frequent updates without republishing the MIB objects. The protocolDirTable in the RMON-2 MIB uses these protocol-identifier strings as index values, allowing a management station to query which protocols are present in monitored traffic and retrieve statistics for each one.

The document notes that auto-discovery of protocols is not explicitly defined by RMON; an agent populates the protocolDirTable with the protocols it has been configured or has discovered. Submissions of new protocol-identifier macros are collected through the RMONMIB working group.
sections.eli5: The RMON table uses these protocol names to keep track of traffic. Monitors can report on any named protocol, and the list of names can grow over time as new protocols are discovered and added to the registry.
